title: What would you need before trusting an AI trading agent with real money?
author: Open_Swimming5859
selftext:
We're building an agentic trading project for the Colosseum hackathon, and feedback from earlier posts has made us rethink quite a few parts of the architecture.

One thing I'm still trying to figure out is where people draw the line between "interesting demo" and "I'd actually let this trade my money."

Our current model is that the agent doesn't get unrestricted wallet access. It gets a limited trading permission with things like a spend cap, and those limits are enforced outside the model.

But even if the agent can't exceed its budget, it can still make terrible trades *inside* that budget.

So for people who have actually run AI/automated trading systems, what would you consider mandatory before letting one trade live?

Things we're currently looking at:

* per-trade limits
* total exposure/spend limits
* slippage protection
* trade-frequency limits
* token/market restrictions
* kill switch
* paper-trading period
* handling duplicate/retried transactions

What am I missing?

Especially interested in cases where the system technically followed all its permissions but still did something stupid economically.

Trying to break as much as possible before the Colosseum submission.

comments.author: Both_Yoghurt1437
comments.body: My trading strategy was built with AI, but I use a trading bot (python script) for my automated trades. There is no AI in the loop.

comments.author: tradematesHQ
comments.body: You're missing a drawdown circuit breaker. Per-trade caps don't stop an agent from bleeding 20 small losses in a row, so halt the whole thing on cumulative loss, not just per-trade size.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Your list covers the mechanical limits well. What's usually missing is the economic ones: a max loss per day and per week that halts trading (not just a spend cap), a check on price versus an independent reference so it won't trade into a stale or manipulated quote, and a minimum liquidity or maximum market-impact rule, since "within budget" can still mean buying a thin market at a terrible price. Also useful are a record of why each trade was made (inputs and timestamps), a comparison of live fills with what the agent expected, and a cool-down after consecutive losses. Event windows (CPI, FOMC, token unlocks) are where a permitted trade goes wrong, and Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for macro releases) is one source for a no-trade filter.

comments.author: TheAgentFloor
comments.body:
I think you are already doing the most important thing, which is keeping the limits outside the agent so it cannot talk itself past them. For me the line between a demo and real money comes down to a few things:

1. Hard limits the agent cannot change, like a max budget, a max order size and a list of what it is allowed to trade.
2. A clear approval setting. Either approve every trade, or approve the rules once and let it act inside them.
3. A kill switch that works instantly and does not depend on the agent cooperating.
4. A plain record of every trade and why the agent made it, written so a normal person can follow it.
5. Permissions that expire. An approval from three months ago may not fit the market today.

For what it is worth, the retail brokers that have opened up to agents mostly handle the first part the way you describe. Robinhood puts the agent in a separate account funded with only what you choose, and Coinbase lets you wall it off in its own portfolio.

One thing I am curious about. Say the agent wants to make a trade that would go over its budget. Does it just skip the trade, or does it ping the user and ask first?

comments.author: murdocc007
comments.body:
How about not using ai for trading. We use ai to create strategies which are deterministic and you can set your own thresholds. 

Check out [wallstreetclaws.com](http://wallstreetclaws.com)

comments.author: ApartmentOk3498
comments.body: drawdown breaker feels mandatory, and keep ai on the esearch/signal side with prospero while execution stays rule based
